title: Liver Glycogenolysis

reactions.name: Glycogen phosphorolysis
reactions.notes: Glycogen (n residues) + Pi → glycogen (n-1 residues) + glucose-1-phosphate. Phosphorolysis, not hydrolysis: the phosphate is incorporated directly, avoiding the cost of ATP. Cleaves alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds sequentially from the non-reducing ends. Stops 4 residues from each alpha-1,6 branch point; debranching enzyme must act before phosphorylase can continue. GPa (phosphorylated form, active); GPb (unphosphorylated form, low activity). In liver, GPa is also directly inhibited allosterically by glucose.

reactions.name: Branch removal
reactions.notes: The debranching enzyme has two distinct catalytic activities on a single polypeptide. (1) 4-alpha-glucanotransferase (EC 2.4.1.25): transfers a trisaccharide from the branch to an adjacent chain, exposing the single alpha-1,6-linked glucose. (2) Amylo-1,6-glucosidase (EC 3.2.1.33): hydrolyses the alpha-1,6 bond, releasing free glucose (not glucose-1-phosphate). Approximately 8-10% of glycogen glucose is released as free glucose by this route.

reactions.name: Glucose-1-phosphate isomerisation
reactions.notes: Glucose-1-phosphate → glucose-6-phosphate. Reversible, near-equilibrium reaction. PGM is constitutively active and not a regulated step. Glucose-1,6-bisphosphate is an obligatory intermediate.

reactions.name: Glucose-6-phosphate hydrolysis
reactions.notes: Glucose-6-phosphate + H2O → glucose + Pi. Rate-limiting for hepatic glucose output. Absent in muscle, so muscle glycogenolysis produces G6P for local glycolysis only, not for export. Gene transcription is induced by glucagon and repressed by insulin.

regulationRules.mechanism: Glucagon → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA. PKA phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase (activates it) and simultaneously phosphorylates inhibitor-1 (activates it, inhibiting protein phosphatase-1). Active phosphorylase kinase phosphorylates GPb on Ser14 → GPa (fully active). This is a classical second-messenger amplification cascade: one glucagon molecule eventually activates ~10,000 phosphorylase molecules.

Adrenaline (epinephrine) binds beta-adrenergic receptors on hepatocytes, raising cAMP via the same adenylyl cyclase cascade as glucagon. Also activates alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, raising intracellular Ca2+, which activates calmodulin-dependent phosphorylase kinase independently of cAMP. Adrenaline is the dominant glycogenolysis signal during acute stress and exercise.

AMP allosterically activates GPb (the unphosphorylated, normally less active form) by binding to the allosteric site, inducing a conformational change toward the active R-state. This provides a hormonal-independent, energy-sensing activation of glycogenolysis when the cell is depleted of ATP (e.g., during intense muscle contraction). In liver, this effect is less dominant than the glucagon/PKA cascade.

Insulin activates protein phosphatase-1 (PP1) by inactivating its inhibitor (inhibitor-1) via Akt-mediated dephosphorylation. PP1 dephosphorylates GPa → GPb, reducing phosphorylase activity. Insulin simultaneously activates glycogen synthase by dephosphorylation, redirecting G6P toward glycogen synthesis.

Liver-specific allosteric regulation: glucose binds to GPa, shifting the equilibrium toward the T-state (less active) and making GPa a better substrate for PP1-mediated dephosphorylation. This glucose-mediated inactivation of GPa occurs in parallel with insulin signalling and provides a feed-forward brake on glycogenolysis when portal glucose rises in the fed state.

teachingSequence: After a meal, the liver accumulates glycogen (up to ~100 g) as a glucose buffer. During fasting, this store is mobilised to maintain blood glucose.
Glucagon is secreted by pancreatic alpha-cells when blood glucose falls. It binds hepatocyte G-protein-coupled receptors, activating adenylyl cyclase and raising cAMP.

cAMP activates PKA, which phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase. Simultaneously, PKA phosphorylates inhibitor-1, which then inhibits protein phosphatase-1, locking the system in the active state.
Phosphorylase kinase phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase b (GPb) → GPa (active). GPa cleaves alpha-1,4 bonds from non-reducing ends, releasing glucose-1-phosphate.

Because phosphorylase cannot cleave within 4 residues of a branch point, debranching enzyme transfers the trisaccharide stub and hydrolyses the remaining alpha-1,6-linked glucose, releasing free glucose directly.
Phosphoglucomutase isomerises G1P to G6P. In the liver (but not muscle), glucose-6-phosphatase in the ER membrane dephosphorylates G6P to free glucose, which exits via GLUT2.
Hepatic glycogen is typically depleted within 12-16 h of fasting, after which gluconeogenesis becomes the sole source of hepatic glucose output.
clinicalLinks: McArdle disease (GSD type V): muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. Painful muscle cramps and myoglobinuria on exercise. Hepatic phosphorylase is normal so fasting blood glucose is maintained. Illustrates that muscle phosphorylase is a different isoenzyme (PYGM vs PYGL).
Hers disease (GSD type VI): liver glycogen phosphorylase (PYGL) deficiency. Mild fasting hypoglycaemia; hepatomegaly. Compensated partly by gluconeogenesis.
GSD type IX: phosphorylase kinase deficiency. The most common GSD. Phosphorylase is present but cannot be activated; similar but milder phenotype to GSD VI.
Glucagonoma: glucagon-secreting pancreatic tumour causing hyperglycaemia partly via uncontrolled glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
DKA and T1DM: absolute insulin deficiency removes the brake on glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; both contribute to severe hyperglycaemia.
